en: Have you come, bloodthirsty Bakai?
Bakai, you slave, hiding yourself in Keng-Kol,
The ill-fated widow
You helped flee Keng-Kol on foot.
You sent her over Zhorgonun-Bel,
That bitch who brought calamity,
You helped flee Talas on foot.
He made known to that slave Bakay.
Did you think you would never disappear?
Bakai, hiding yourself in Talas,
My child left by Manas
You helped escape toward Temir Khan.
You filled my offspring with rancor,
And attacked those left to me.
That your death has come,
Do you know, mighty Bakai?
Your tricks have failed today!
Allah has delivered you into my hands;
Bakai has come because his death is due!
Shaggy Bakai, you slave,
I shall dig your pit this instant,
Bakai, you slave, brew your misery this instant!
I shall work a wonder now,
Binding your hands behind your back.
I shall show you, Bakai, you slave,
A wonder no human has seen.
I shall strip off and take as booty
The coat you wear, obtained so late in life!”
So saying, Khan Zhakyp
Turned and made ready.
Speaking harsh and chilling words,
Zhakyp was struck astray by God again.
No life is visible.
King Bakai, the noble lion,
Then spoke to the swine khan:
“I came to look you in the eye.
Look, you swine, I came seeking you yourself.
Listen to the words I now speak!
I came to strip the hair from your head,
I came to cut off your head.
I came to draw the line,
I came to bring upon you
Mischief no human would devise.
I came to hear your words,
I mean to gouge out, swine khan,
Those two sunken eyes of yours.
When my sovereign Manas died,
My white steel was chipped.
Now his lion has come, and Bakai's
Strength and condition have been restored.
I hid myself in Talas;
What you said is true as well.
The child I took as my refuge,
I helped flee Talas on foot.
I hid myself in Keng-Kol,
Fearing evil would befall him,
While he was still an infant,
Fearing death would come to him needlessly,
Fearing you would do your worst—
It is true that I suffered.
My orphan has come; I am restored.
My exposed flesh is covered;
My honor has thus been regained.
Beware, my anger will rise!
I shall kill you yourself.
I shall not heed your commanding words;
I shall gouge out your eyes this instant.
I shall begin turmoil against you,
Work wonders all at once.
Now that my precious orphan has come,
Now that God has granted my wish,
Great Talas with its springs and valleys—
I have no herds to drive upcountry.
Let my own kinsmen turn against me;
I have no life to spare from death.
Tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol, broad Talas—
I have no herds to drive onward.
If an enemy rises from level ground,
I have no life to hold back.
Hardened by drinking blood,
I became known as Bakai the Leopard.
I have recovered my former state;
My orphan has come, and I am mighty.
If a troublesome khan appears,
I shall plunder his fine cloth.
If anyone talks back,
Watch, swine khan:
I shall slaughter him as a sacrifice!
My support has come; I am restored.
Now I shall take my long-standing revenge!
I shall move my camp up Talas,
And take the late Manas as my support.
Today I shall turn my thoughts to joy,
Take as my refuge
The child left by Manas.
Today, Zhakyp, my orphan has come; I am restored.
Thus I have rejoined the ranks.
All humiliation has vanished;
Today lamenting Bakai has recovered.
I mean to claim equality.
I mean to perform against you
My feats of long ago.
Let me show before your eyes
My lion-like valor as of old.
Today let me trample upon your head,
You God-stricken swine khan,
Let me scatter your four kinds of livestock.
Will he not dig your road to doom,
Let me strip off and wear as booty
The coat upon your back.
Let me put an end to your replies;
Let me dig your pit deep.
Let me strip away your secrets.
You have boiled up all my rage.
Swine khan, let me end your quarrels.
My misfortune that has gone so far?
I shall seize back as booty
My property left by the formidable one.
I shall kill you yourself.
If you stir my anger, I shall gouge out
Those glistening eyes of yours.
Today I shall drink your liquor and consume your food.
If you provoke my stubborn temper too far,
I shall cut off your head.
I have come to ask
How old you have grown.
Camel-herding Bakai has recovered;
The lord's son, dear Semetey, has grown.
Fugitive Bakai has recovered;
Today the dear leopard has grown.
Now I shall move my camp from Keng-Kol.
From those swaggering dogs
I, Bakai, mean to take
My long-standing revenge.
They scattered my people from Talas;
Wandering Bakai has recovered.
I, Bakai, mean to avenge
My suffering of long ago.
All my sorrow has diminished;
My wings have grown a span.
My orphan has been found upon the plain;
My honor has thus been covered.
To grapple, I, Bakai,
Now go about in readiness.
At the property you refuse when asked,
I shall cast a cold lasso.
The treasure you refuse when requested,
I shall force you to yield and seize.
Now that God has given me support,
Watch, Khan Zhakyp:
I shall bring turmoil upon you.
My horses in the hills have mottled heads,
Argymaks and fine steeds mingled.
Where is my property, Khan Zhakyp?
My horses in the mountains are nine vast herds,
Toburchaks and swift steeds mingled.
Where is this livestock of mine, Khan Zhakyp?
Taking battle-ax and sword in hand,
I have come to torment you.
The property you plundered,
I have come to demand from you.
Human decency and honor,
I have come to cast aside.
If you give way to your old madness,
Mischief no human would devise,
I have come to begin with you.
You burned Ken-Kol,
Since my caravan, Manas, departed,
You did something to me I shall never forget.
You camped up along Talas,
And exchanged fire with me worse than the Manchu.
Zulpukor, never sated with blood—
Watch, Khan Zhakyp:
I have come to grapple.
As with the Black Chinese and Manchu,
With you, Khan Zhakyp,
I have come to fight.
Tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol, broad Talas—
I have come to take land.
Name the place where you will fight.
Against you, Khan Zhakyp,
I have come to take revenge.
Marking out and measuring your land,
I have come to settle.
Be seven together with your sons;
I have come to exchange fire with you.
When some terrible thing to Manas
I have come to do it.
If you have sense, Khan Zhakyp,
Father of my khan, Khan Manas,
If you yourself are good,
I have come to pitch camp in Talas,
And dwell here.
If you play the devil, Khan Zhakyp,
With you, I myself
Have come to fight.
When I dismount in respect for an elder,
The black gun Zulpukor
You stand ready to aim.
“Where are Abyke's sixty warriors?” you ask,
And stand ready to wage war.
Your boar-like sons are six;
You stand ready to gather them.
Such is your swinish nature:
You stand ready to fight.
Saddle-sore from herding camels,
I have a short-tailed mount beneath me.
May God now strike all sixty,
Even now I have strength enough for you!”
When he heard Bakai's words,
Khan Zhakyp, cunning beyond measure,
Let a wind of words blow from his mouth.
Hearing that Semetey had come,
He meant to play a trick on Khan Bakai.
In this swine's house
There was bozo in a leather bucket,
To shake one down like a blossom,
With burning poison mixed into it.
In this fool's house
There was bozo in a wooden tub;
One who smelled it would die.
Potent poison was mixed as well.
To contrive to deceive him,
To Manas's only son Semetey,
To give it to that orphan slave,
He falsely wept with ringing cries,
And pleaded with Khan Bakai.
Hearing news of the boy,
He merely pretended to weep and wail.
“Ah, my cherished Khan Bakai,
Has the orphan truly come?
Has God granted my wish?
Now that my beard is white,
Now that my departure is at hand,
At the time when I must die,
That river and spring in the valley,
Bring him over here,
That dear one found late in life,
That firmly rooted poplar and plane tree,
My only one left by Khan Manas,
That lamp, Semetey!
That tender gray-mottled falcon
I have been asking God for,
That morning star left by my son Manas.
I go on living for that soul,
For the boy Semetey alone.
For whom have I stayed alive?
To Temir Khan's city
He wandered and grew up—
For that boy Semetey alone.
“My reed and mint in the water,
My only one left by Sultan Manas!
Longing before God,
I kept making a vow:
Let me see Semetey,
And after that let me die.
